content.title: About
content.content: Bean paste, sweetened is a thick paste made from cooked beans and sweetened with sugar or other sweeteners. It is widely used in Asian cuisine, especially in Japanese, Korean and Chinese desserts, as well as in baking and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally the paste is made from red azuki beans, but other bean varieties can be used.
In Japan the sweet bean paste is called “anko” and is considered a fundamental sweet ingredient.
The paste is often used as a filling for mochi, dango, rolls and bento boxes.
There are two main types: “tsuba‑anko” (coarse) and “kitsu‑anko” (smooth).
It can be stored in the refrigerator for several weeks and frozen for up to a year.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide a notable amount of protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The paste contains thiamine, riboflavin and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sweet spreads, sweet bean paste is low in fat.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals in beans help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The paste is often heavily sweetened, so people with diabetes or those monitoring sugar intake should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beans, experiencing skin rashes, swelling or respiratory issues.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; large amounts of paste should be balanced with other foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet bean paste is used as a filling for buns, rolls, pancakes and cakes, added to sauces, ice cream, or simply eaten by the spoonful as a dessert. It can be gently warmed to become more pliable.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the paste in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. For longer storage, freeze in small portions where it will retain quality for up to 12 months. Before use, check for any off‑smell indicating fermentation.

content.title: About
content.content: Gummy candy is a sweet treat made from gelatin, sugar, fruit or berry flavorings, and colorants. It has a soft, chewy texture and a bright, fruity flavor profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first gummy-like sweets appeared in ancient Rome, using honey and fish-derived gelatin.
Modern gummies often use plant‑based gelling agents such as pectin instead of animal gelatin.
Bright colors are frequently obtained from natural extracts, but mass production relies on synthetic food dyes.
In Japan, “gummy‑med” coated with powdered sugar change flavor as you chew.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The sugar provides a rapid increase in blood glucose, delivering an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Fruit flavorings may contribute a small amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Sweet taste stimulates serotonin production, helping to improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to weight gain, tooth decay, and blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Gelatin allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to gelatin, especially when it is animal‑derived.

items.title: Synthetic colorants
items.content: Certain food dyes have been linked to hyperactivity in children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Gummy candy is convenient as a standalone snack, can be added to dessert mixes, used in baking, or as decorative toppings for cakes and cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight package, protecting from moisture and direct sunlight. Properly stored, they retain shape and flavor for up to 12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Cottonseed oil is extracted from the seeds of the cotton plant (Gossypium spp.). It is a light‑yellow vegetable oil with a neutral taste and aroma. The oil is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, especially linoleic acid, and is widely used in cooking, food processing, and cosmetics.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottonseed oil is one of the cheapest vegetable oils worldwide.
Cotton seeds contain about 20 % oil, which is obtained by pressing and solvent extraction.
More than 70 % of the world’s cottonseed oil production occurs in the United States.
The oil is commonly used in margarines, mayonnaise, and sauces because of its high oxidative stability when stored properly.
In cosmetics, cottonseed oil is valued for its gentle moisturizing properties and ability to improve product texture.

items.title: Rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids
items.content: Linoleic acid in cottonseed oil supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Skin support
items.content: The oil is often used in skin care to improve barrier function and reduce dryness.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with some other vegetable oils, cottonseed oil contains less saturated fatty acids.

items.title: Contains phytosterols
items.content: Phytosterols may help lower blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Cotton seeds are frequently treated with pesticides; choose refined, quality‑checked oil.

items.title: Cotton allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to components of the oil.

items.title: High omega‑6 content
items.content: Excessive intake of omega‑6 fatty acids can disrupt the omega‑3/omega‑6 balance, which is undesirable for health.

items.title: Trans fats from improper processing
items.content: Unrefined or overheated oil can form trans fats, which are harmful to the heart.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Cottonseed oil is suitable for frying, baking, making sauces and marinades. It can replace more expensive oils in recipes. In cosmetics, it is used in hair masks, moisturizing creams, and lotions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the oil in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it refrigerated to prevent oxidation. Discard oil that has a rancid smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Gluten‑free crackers are crisp snack biscuits made from gluten‑free grains such as rice, corn or buckwheat and flavored with a variety of seasonings like cheese, herbs or spices. They are suitable for people with celiac disease and anyone following a gluten‑free diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free crackers are often used as a base for canapés and bite‑size appetizers.
Flavorings can be natural (herbs, spices) or artificial, but are always listed on the label.
Compared with whole‑grain crackers, gluten‑free versions may have lower fiber content, so they are frequently fortified with vitamins and minerals.
In many countries gluten‑free products must carry the “gluten‑free” label according to international standards.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Gluten‑free grains like rice and corn are easier to digest for those sensitive to gluten, reducing the risk of intestinal irritation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most gluten‑free crackers are baked with little added fat, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Fortified varieties may contain thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Some recipes include added iron, calcium or magnesium, beneficial for bones and muscles.

items.title: Hypoallergenic
items.content: The absence of gluten makes these crackers safe for individuals with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Crackers may contain soy sauce, dairy flavorings or nuts, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Flavored versions often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Reduced fiber
items.content: Compared with whole‑grain products, gluten‑free crackers can have less dietary fiber, affecting satiety.

items.title: Potential additives
items.content: Some flavorings may be artificial; if preferred, select products labeled with “natural flavor.”

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Gluten‑free crackers can be enjoyed as a snack on their own, paired with cheese, hummus, pâtés, or used as a base for mini‑sandwiches. Lightly warming them in the oven can enhance their crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. Once opened, consume within 2–3 weeks to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Pine nuts are the small, creamy-white, elongated edible seeds found inside the cones of certain pine trees, such as the stone pine, Korean pine, and Siberian pine. They have a delicate, buttery, slightly sweet and resinous flavor. Pine nuts are eaten raw or toasted and used in pesto, salads, pilafs, baked goods, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pine nuts are seeds harvested from pine cones, and extracting them is labor-intensive, which makes them expensive.
Different pine species produce pine nuts, including the stone pine of the Mediterranean and the Korean and Siberian pines of Asia.
Pine nuts are the traditional ingredient in pesto genovese.
Toasting pine nuts lightly brings out their buttery flavor.
Some people experience a bitter or metallic taste for days after eating certain pine nuts, a condition called pine mouth.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Pine nuts contain mostly unsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Provides vitamin E and vitamin K
items.content: These vitamins support antioxidant protection and blood clotting.

items.title: Provides magnesium, manganese, and zinc
items.content: These minerals support muscle function, metabolism, and immune function.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: Pine nuts provide protein and some fiber.

items.title: Contains pinolenic acid
items.content: Pine nuts contain a distinctive fatty acid that is being studied.

items.title: Pine mouth
items.content: Some people develop a bitter or metallic taste lasting a few days to weeks after eating pine nuts. It is harmless but unpleasant, and it usually goes away on its own.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pine nuts can cause allergic reactions in people with nut allergies.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Pine nuts are calorie-dense, so portions should be small.

items.title: Rancidity
items.content: Pine nuts have a lot of oil and turn rancid quickly, so discard nuts that smell or taste bitter or off.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pine nuts can be toasted lightly in a dry pan until golden and added to salads, pilafs, pasta, and vegetables, or blended into pesto and sauces. They can also be added to baked goods and desserts. Use them in small amounts and watch them closely when toasting, because they burn quickly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pine nuts in an airtight container in the refrigerator or freezer, since their oils turn rancid quickly. Use shelled pine nuts within a few months. Discard nuts that smell rancid or taste bitter.

content.title: About
content.content: A sour dough roll is a soft, lightly toasted bread roll made with a natural sourdough starter. The starter gives it a distinctive tangy aroma, improves crumb structure, and makes the product more nutritious.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The starter contains live lactic‑acid bacteria and yeasts that naturally leaven the dough.
Traditionally these rolls are baked in bakeries that maintain a continuous “starter” from previous batches.
Sourdough dough oxidizes more slowly, so the roll stays fresh longer.
The acidity of the starter enhances mineral absorption from the grain.
Sourdough rolls often have a more open, airy crumb compared with yeast‑based versions.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Live microorganisms in the starter support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Fermentation slows carbohydrate absorption, helping to regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Sourdough fermentation produces B1, B2 and B3 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Improves digestion
items.content: Enzymes formed during fermentation aid in breaking down starches and proteins.

items.title: Enhances mineral bioavailability
items.content: The acidic environment reduces phytates, allowing better absorption of iron, zinc and magnesium.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: As with any wheat product, rolls can trigger reactions in people with gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes add salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of unwanted bacteria, especially at room temperature.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: People with high stomach acidity may experience discomfort from the tangy flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sourdough rolls are perfect for sandwiches, as a side to soups, or as a base for open‑face toppings. They can be toasted and topped with butter, cheese, ham, or fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the roll in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, place it in an airtight container in the refrigerator – up to 5 days. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Tea is an infusion made from the leaves, buds or flowers of the Camellia sinensis plant. Kombucha is a fermented beverage produced by the joint fermentation of tea, sugar and a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast (SCOBY). Both products are popular for their taste and potential health benefits.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tea is the second most consumed beverage in the world after water.
There are more than 3,000 tea varieties, distinguished by processing methods.
Kombucha has been known in Asia for over 2,000 years and traditionally used as a tonic.
During fermentation kombucha produces a small amount of alcohol (usually less than 0.5 %).
The SCOBY looks like a jelly‑like “mushroom,” but it is not a fungus; it is a colony of bacteria and yeast.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tea, especially green tea, is rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Kombucha contains probiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Improved hydration
items.content: Both drinks contribute to maintaining the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Blood sugar regulation
items.content: Some studies suggest tea polyphenols may improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: B‑vitamins and organic acids in kombucha may help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Black and green teas contain caffeine, which can cause anxiety or sleep disturbances in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Tea leaf allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Kombucha contamination
items.content: Improper fermentation can lead to growth of pathogenic microbes and higher alcohol content.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Kombucha’s low pH may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Caffeine and certain tea compounds can amplify the effects of stimulants or anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steep tea in hot (not boiling) water for 2–5 minutes, depending on the type. Kombucha is usually consumed chilled; it can be diluted with water or flavored with fruit juices and spices. Both beverages are suitable for breakfast, snacks, or as a refreshing evening drink.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tea in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place, protected from moisture and odors. Keep kombucha refrigerated in a sealed bottle for 1–2 weeks; discard it if mold or off‑flavors appear.
